html:
Around 525 the Christian king Kaleb of Aksum sent an army across the Red Sea, overthrew Dhu Nuwas, the Jewish king of Himyar in Yemen, and put South Arabia under Aksumite control.

Himyar had ruled most of southern Arabia for centuries. Its kings had adopted a form of Judaism, while Christian communities grew in towns such as Najran. Around 523 Dhu Nuwas attacked the Christians of Najran and killed many of them. News of the massacre spread through the Christian world, and the Roman emperor Justin I encouraged Aksum, a fellow Christian power, to act.

Kaleb's victory made Aksum master of both shores of the southern Red Sea, a key link in the trade between the Roman Empire and India. But control slipped. An Aksumite commander, Abraha, seized power in Yemen and ruled almost on his own. Arab tradition says he marched on Mecca with an elephant in the "Year of the Elephant", the year Muhammad was born.

Around 570 the Sasanian Persians drove the Aksumites out of Yemen. Aksum, cut off from Arabia, began its long decline.
sum: Around 525 the Christian king Kaleb of Aksum sent an army across the Red Sea, overthrew Dhu Nuwas, the Jewish king of Himyar in Yemen, and put South Arabia under Aksumite control.
